fatal_errors: The proposed material and intervention are fundamentally different from the target: uncoated Q235 is annealed at 800 °C rather than applying an AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating to SS316L and annealing it at 550 °C for 2 h.

The cited evidence concerns Al- and Cr-bearing eutectic HEA coatings, so it cannot substantiate formation of an analogous protective Fe-oxide scale on low-alloy Q235 or protection in room-temperature NaCl.
The annealing atmosphere is unspecified even though the hypothesis requires controlled growth of an oxide scale; annealing in vacuum, inert gas, or air would produce fundamentally different surfaces.
The proposed conditions disagree with the target regimes: 750 °C instead of 900 °C hot corrosion, NaCl solution instead of 3.5 wt% H2SO4, and omission of the V2O5-containing salts.
The duration series does not isolate oxide-scale causality because annealing time simultaneously changes substrate microstructure, residual stress, and scale properties.
explanation: The response is testable and broadly addresses retention or loss of protection across hot-salt and aqueous regimes. Its oxide continuity-versus-spallation concept has limited qualitative consistency with the cited hot-corrosion evidence, and the untreated material is a reasonable reference for its own proposed study. Nevertheless, it does not reconstruct the central HEA-coating intervention, optimum annealing condition, Al/Cr-rich passive-scale chemistry, or specified electrochemical and hot-corrosion conditions. The cited study only shows that Al2O3-, Cr2O3-, and spinel-containing scales on HEA coatings can differ in spallation and mass loss; it does not support the claimed behavior of an annealed Fe-oxide scale on Q235, especially at room temperature. The falsification experiment is also correlational rather than decisively causal. A stronger design would control annealing atmosphere, compare oxide-retained and oxide-stripped specimens with matched heat histories, and include coated/as-sprayed and uncoated references.
